title: Magic, Stories and the Silent Era
summary: A Paris magician named Georges Méliès discovered he could stop his camera and make people vanish, then sent a rocket crashing into the Moon's eye. Alice Guy filmed a fairy finding babies in a cabbage patch, and soon whole cities were packing into five-cent theaters. Silent films were never really silent: a piano or a mighty organ played along in the dark!

sections.heading: The Magician Who Wanted a Camera
paragraphs: Paris, 27 December 1895. In a room at the Grand Café, the Lumière brothers are giving a private demonstration of their Cinématographe, the night before their first paid public show. Among the invited guests sits a 34-year-old man with a neat beard and a showman's sparkle in his eyes. His name is Georges Méliès. When the flickering grey pictures of workers and street scenes appear on the screen, he is thunderstruck. Afterwards he goes straight to the Lumières' father, Antoine, and offers to buy a machine. According to the usual account he offered 10,000 francs, a huge sum. The answer was no. The Lumières wanted to control their invention themselves.

Méliès was born in Paris on 8 December 1861, the son of a wealthy boot manufacturer. His family expected him to join the shoe business, but he loved drawing, puppets and above all stage magic. While in London as a young man he visited the Egyptian Hall, a famous home of conjuring shows, and was hooked. In 1888 he used his share of the family fortune to buy the Théâtre Robert-Houdin in Paris, a small magic theatre founded by the great French magician Jean-Eugène Robert-Houdin. There Méliès performed illusions, built mechanical gadgets and designed elaborate stage tricks in which people vanished, floated or lost their heads.

Refused by the Lumières, Méliès did not give up. In early 1896 he travelled to London and bought a projector called the Animatograph from the British inventor Robert W. Paul. Back in Paris he and his mechanics rebuilt it to work as a camera too. By April 1896 his theatre was showing films between the magic acts, and soon he was shooting his own. Later that year he founded a company with the bold name Star Film, whose trademark was a star, and in September 1896 he began building one of the first film studios in the world, in the garden of his family property at Montreuil, just outside Paris.

The Montreuil studio looked like a giant greenhouse. Its walls and roof were made of glass, because film of the time needed enormous amounts of light, and electric lighting strong enough was not yet practical. Inside was a stage like a theatre's, with trapdoors, pulleys and painted backdrops. Méliès painted most of the scenery himself, usually in shades of grey, because the film of the time was black and white and real colours often photographed in strange ways. He was producer, writer, designer, director, actor and special-effects expert all at once.

sections.heading: A Bus That Turned into a Hearse
paragraphs: Méliès liked to tell a story about how he discovered his greatest trick, and it is a wonderful tale, though we only have his own word for it. One day, he said, he was filming traffic in a Paris street when his camera jammed. It took him about a minute to fix it and start cranking again. When he developed the film and projected it, he saw something astonishing. During that minute, the street had changed. A horse-drawn bus seemed to transform, in an instant, into a hearse, a carriage for carrying coffins, and men seemed to turn into women. Whether or not it happened just like that, it makes a good legend about the birth of the special effect.

The trick that the story describes is called the stop trick, or substitution. It works because of exactly what you learned in the last part: film is a row of still frames. Stop the camera, change something in front of it, keep everything else perfectly in place, and start the camera again. When the film is projected, the change happens between one frame and the next, in one twenty-fourth of a second or less, and it looks like magic. A magician can make a lady vanish on stage only by using hidden trapdoors and mirrors. With a camera, Méliès could make her disappear by simply stopping, asking her to walk away, and starting again. To make the join seamless, he would often cut the film at the exact frame and glue the pieces together, an early form of the careful editing we now call a substitution splice.

Méliès went much further. He discovered multiple exposure: he would film a scene with part of the lens covered in black, wind the film back, uncover that part, cover the rest and film again. In The One-Man Band (1900) he played seven musicians at the same time, all of them him. In The Man with the Rubber Head (1901) his own head swells to an enormous size; he achieved this by moving himself towards the camera on a sliding cart and combining the shot with another. He used dissolves, in which one scene slowly fades into another, and he made objects appear, vanish and transform. Many of his films were sold in colour versions that were hand-painted, frame by frame, by teams of women working with tiny brushes and dyes, in a workshop he hired for the job.

Between 1896 and 1913 Méliès made more than 500 films. Most were only a minute or a few minutes long, but they were packed with devils, fairies, skeletons, mermaids, exploding characters and transformations. People sometimes call him the father of special effects, and though others also invented film tricks, no one in those years used them with such wild imagination.

sections.heading: A Rocket in the Moon's Eye
paragraphs: In 1902 Méliès made the film that is still his most famous: Le Voyage dans la Lune, or A Trip to the Moon. It took about three months to make and cost about 10,000 francs, a fortune for a film at the time. The story borrows ideas from Jules Verne's novels From the Earth to the Moon and Around the Moon, and perhaps from H. G. Wells's The First Men in the Moon, which had just come out. A club of bearded astronomers in robes and pointed hats, led by Professor Barbenfouillis, played by Méliès himself, decides to fly to the Moon. Workers build a giant cannon on the rooftops. The astronomers climb into a bullet-shaped capsule and are fired into space.

Then comes the most famous image in early cinema. The Moon, shown as a round face in the sky, grows larger and larger as the capsule approaches, and the rocket lands with a splat right in its eye. On the Moon the explorers watch the Earth rise, sleep under the stars, and wander through a cave of giant mushrooms. They meet the Selenites, Moon creatures with insect-like bodies, played by acrobats from the Folies Bergère theatre in Paris. When a scientist bonks a Selenite with his umbrella, it explodes in a puff of smoke, another stop trick. The explorers escape, tumble back to Earth, splash into the sea, and return home as heroes.

A Trip to the Moon was a hit all over Europe and America. Sadly for Méliès, much of the money went to others. Copying a film was easy, and copyright laws had not caught up with the new invention. Companies in the United States, including Thomas Edison's company and others run by Siegmund Lubin and William Selig, made copies of Méliès's films and sold them without paying him. This piracy was one reason Méliès sent his brother Gaston to open an American branch of Star Film in New York in 1903, and why he began stamping his star trademark into the scenery of his films.

For about a century, people believed the hand-coloured version of A Trip to the Moon had vanished forever. Then in 1993 a coloured print turned up at the Filmoteca de Catalunya, the film archive of Catalonia in Spain. It was in terrible condition; the nitrate had decayed so badly that the reels were almost a solid lump. Over many years, restorers led by the French company Lobster Films carefully separated and copied fragments, frame by frame, then used digital tools to rebuild missing parts. The work cost about 1 million US dollars. In 2011 the restored colour film was shown at the Cannes Film Festival, 109 years after it was made, with a new soundtrack by the French band Air. That same year, Martin Scorsese's film Hugo, based on a novel by Brian Selznick, introduced Méliès and his Moon to a whole new generation of children.

sections.heading: Alice Guy and the Cabbage Fairy
paragraphs: While Méliès was building his glass studio, another French pioneer was quietly changing what films could be. Alice Guy was born in 1873 near Paris and grew up partly in Chile, where her father ran bookshops. As a young woman she learned typing and shorthand, then new skills for women entering offices, and in 1894 she became the secretary to Léon Gaumont at a company that sold photographic equipment. Gaumont's company soon began making its own film cameras and projectors.

In 1895 Alice Guy went with Gaumont to a Lumière demonstration. The Lumière films, like most early films, mostly showed real life: workers leaving a factory, a train arriving, a baby eating breakfast. Guy thought films could do more. They could tell invented stories, like little plays. She asked Gaumont whether she could make some films herself, as long as it did not interfere with her secretarial work. He agreed, reportedly thinking it was a harmless hobby.

Her first film was La Fée aux Choux, The Cabbage Fairy, made in 1896. It was about a minute long and drew on an old French folk tale in which babies are found growing in cabbage patches, much like the English story that babies are brought by storks. Historians still argue about the details, because the original 1896 version is lost. Alice Guy herself said she remade the story at least twice, and versions from 1900 and 1902 survive, showing a fairy in a white dress lifting real babies out of a garden of cabbages. Whatever the exact date, she is widely credited as one of the very first people, and the first woman, to direct fiction films: films with a planned story, actors and sets.

Guy soon became head of film production at Gaumont, a job she held until 1906. She wrote, directed and supervised hundreds of films, including comedies, fairy tales, dance films and a long Life of Christ in 1906 with hundreds of extras. She also experimented with Gaumont's Chronophone, a system that played sound recordings on a phonograph alongside the film, making some of the earliest synchronized music films, more than twenty years before the talkies.

sections.heading: Train Robbers and Nickel Theatres
paragraphs: In 1907 Alice Guy married Herbert Blaché, a British cameraman who worked for Gaumont, and the couple moved to the United States. In 1910 Alice Guy-Blaché co-founded her own company, Solax, and in 1912 she built a modern studio in Fort Lee, New Jersey, across the river from New York City, which was then the busiest filmmaking town in America. On the studio wall, it is said, hung a big sign with her advice to actors: Be Natural. Her Solax film A Fool and His Money (1912) is thought to be the first film with an all-African-American cast. Over her career she made hundreds of films; estimates range from several hundred to around a thousand, though many are lost. After her marriage ended she returned to France in 1922 and never directed again. She was largely forgotten for decades, received France's Legion of Honour in 1958, and died in New Jersey in 1968. A 2018 documentary, Be Natural, helped bring her story back to light.

Meanwhile American filmmakers were learning to tell exciting stories. In November 1903 Edwin S. Porter, a camera operator and director working for the Edison Manufacturing Company, made The Great Train Robbery. It runs about 12 minutes, long for the time, and follows a gang of outlaws who hold up a railway station, rob a steam train and its passengers, flee on horseback, and are finally caught by a posse. Some scenes were shot in Edison's New York studio, but others were filmed outdoors in New Jersey, including along a real railway line, which made the action feel thrillingly real.

Porter's film is famous for its storytelling. He cut between different places, showing the robbers escaping while, elsewhere, the telegraph operator is found tied up and the townspeople gather, so the audience understood that events were happening at the same time. This technique is called cross-cutting. The film also ends with a shock: a medium close-up of the outlaw leader, played by Justus D. Barnes, pointing his revolver straight at the camera and firing at the audience. The shot has nothing to do with the plot, and cinemas could show it at the start or the end. Some prints were hand-coloured so that gunshot smoke and clothing glowed with colour. It was not the first Western or the first story film, as people sometimes claim, but it was one of the most popular films of its decade.

Where did people see films like this? At first, in vaudeville theatres, fairgrounds and travelling shows. Then on 19 June 1905, in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, two businessmen named Harry Davis and John P. Harris opened a small storefront theatre on Smithfield Street dedicated to moving pictures. They called it the Nickelodeon, from the nickel, the five-cent coin it cost to get in, plus odeon, an old Greek word for a theatre. The Great Train Robbery was among the films audiences flocked to see.

The idea spread like wildfire. Nickelodeons were usually converted shops, narrow and long, with fewer than 200 hard wooden chairs, a piano near the screen and a projector at the back. Programs of short films ran over and over all day, so people could drop in whenever they liked. For working families, and for immigrants who were still learning English, five cents bought an affordable trip into another world. By 1908 there were about 8,000 nickelodeons in the United States, and by 1910 as many as 26 million Americans were going to the movies every week.

sections.heading: Westward to Hollywood, and a Film That Did Harm
paragraphs: In the early 1900s most American films were made around New York and New Jersey. But in 1908 Thomas Edison and other big companies formed the Motion Picture Patents Company, which used its patents on cameras and projectors to try to control who could make films. Independent filmmakers who did not pay could be sued, or have their cameras seized. Southern California offered an escape, as well as many other attractions: bright sunshine almost all year round for filming outdoors, cheap land, and an amazing variety of scenery within a day's journey, including oceans, mountains, deserts, forests and farms.

In early 1910 the director D. W. Griffith brought a film crew west from New York and shot In Old California in the little farming suburb of Hollywood, often called the first film made there. Studios soon followed. By the late 1910s Hollywood had become the movie capital of America, and before long the name Hollywood stood for the American film industry itself.

Griffith became one of the most influential directors of the silent era. Working at the Biograph company from 1908, he directed hundreds of short films and developed a smooth style of storytelling: moving between close-ups that showed actors' faces and wide shots that showed huge scenes, using cross-cutting to build suspense, as when a heroine in danger is shown in one shot and the rescuers racing to save her in the next, and asking actors to perform in a subtle, natural way instead of waving their arms like stage actors. He did not invent all these techniques, but he used them with great skill.

In 1915 Griffith released The Birth of a Nation, a long epic about the American Civil War and the period afterwards, which ran around three hours in some versions. It had enormous battle scenes, a full orchestral score, and was a gigantic commercial success, one of the highest-earning films of the entire silent era. It was also deeply racist. Based on a novel called The Clansman, it presented the Ku Klux Klan, a violent white-supremacist group, as heroes, and portrayed Black Americans, many of them played by white actors in blackface makeup, as dangerous and foolish. The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) organised protests, and the film was banned in some cities and states. Historians agree that it helped inspire the revival of the Ku Klux Klan later in 1915. Today it is studied both for its filmmaking techniques and as a painful example of how powerful moving pictures can spread harmful lies.

sections.heading: Stars, Title Cards and a Piano in the Dark
paragraphs: As films grew longer, audiences began to love particular actors, and the film star was born. Charlie Chaplin, a young English music-hall comedian, made his first film in America in 1914 and that same year created the Little Tramp, a gentle wanderer with a bowler hat, a cane, baggy trousers, oversized shoes and a tiny moustache. Through films such as The Kid (1921) and The Gold Rush (1925), in which the starving Tramp boils and eats his own boot, Chaplin became one of the most famous people on Earth. Buster Keaton, nicknamed the Great Stone Face because he almost never smiled on screen, performed astonishing stunts himself. In The General (1926) he rides a speeding steam locomotive, and in Steamboat Bill, Jr. (1928) the whole front wall of a house falls on him, and he survives because he is standing exactly where an open window lands.

Mary Pickford, born in Canada, was nicknamed America's Sweetheart and was one of the most popular and highest-paid stars in the world. She was also a sharp businesswoman. On 5 February 1919 she founded the company United Artists with Chaplin, the swashbuckling star Douglas Fairbanks, and D. W. Griffith, so the artists could control and profit from their own films. A rival studio boss reportedly joked that 'the inmates are taking over the asylum'.

Silent films had no recorded voices, so how did viewers follow the story? Mostly through acting, faces and gestures, but also through intertitles, printed cards inserted between scenes. Some gave information, such as 'Next morning', while others showed what a character was saying. Writing them became a separate job, and good title writers could make audiences laugh or cry with a few words. Films could even be sold abroad simply by translating the cards. In Japan, a live narrator called a benshi stood beside the screen and explained the story, voiced the characters and added commentary, and the most famous benshi were stars in their own right.

The most common mistake people make about silent films is that they were watched in silence. Almost every show had live music. A small nickelodeon might have a single pianist who watched the screen and changed the tune for chases, love scenes and villains. Bigger cinemas installed theatre organs, such as the famous Wurlitzer, that could imitate a whole orchestra plus sound effects like bells, horns and thunder. The grandest picture palaces of the 1920s had full orchestras. Studios sent out cue sheets suggesting what music to play for each scene, and big films got their own scores. Many films were also tinted with coloured dyes: blue for night, amber for lamplight, red for fire, green for something eerie. By around 1920, an estimated 80 to 90 percent of films had some colour of this kind.

sections.heading: The Lost Films
paragraphs: Here is a sad truth: most of these films are gone. In 2013 the Library of Congress in Washington, D.C., published a study by the film historian David Pierce. He counted 10,919 American silent feature films released between 1912 and 1929 and then searched archives and collections around the world to find which survived. Only 1,575, about 14 percent, exist complete in their original American 35mm form. Another 11 percent survive complete in other forms, such as foreign versions or smaller-gauge copies. About 5 percent survive only in pieces. The remaining 70 percent are believed to be completely lost. Put another way, about 75 percent of the creative record of American silent features either no longer exists or survives only in incomplete form.

Why? Partly because of nitrate, the dangerous film you met in the last part. As it ages it decays into sticky goo and then powder, and vault fires destroyed huge collections, such as the 1937 fire at a Fox storage site and the 1965 fire at MGM that destroyed the last known copy of a famous horror film, London After Midnight (1927). But the biggest reason was simply that nobody thought old films mattered. When sound arrived, silent films seemed worthless overnight. Studios threw prints away, or melted them down to recover the silver in the film. During the First World War, the French army even confiscated many of Méliès's prints and melted them to make material for the war effort. Ruined by debt and changing fashions, Méliès had stopped making films by 1913, and in despair he is said to have destroyed his own stored negatives.

Méliès's story had a gentler ending. For years he ran a small toy and sweet stall at the Montparnasse railway station in Paris, with his second wife, the actress Jehanne d'Alcy, who had appeared in many of his films. In the late 1920s journalists and film fans rediscovered him, a gala of his surviving films was held in Paris in 1929, and in 1931 he was made a Knight of the Legion of Honour, with the medal presented by none other than Louis Lumière. He died in 1938.

Lost films still turn up today. Prints have been found in attics, in foreign archives where American films had been sent decades earlier, and in strange places. In 2008 a nearly complete copy of Fritz Lang's German science-fiction epic Metropolis (1927), with scenes missing for about 80 years, was found in a museum in Buenos Aires, Argentina. Every discovery is like opening a time capsule. Each one also reminds us of the colours that were often missing from these silver-grey films. Audiences in the 1910s and 1920s watched heroes and villains in a world of black, white and tinted shades, and many longed for the day they could see the true red of a rose and the deep blue of the sky on the screen.

deepDive: The silent era is full of disputed 'firsts', and historians have become cautious about them. Alice Guy-Blaché is often called the first director of a fiction film, but the Lumières' L'Arroseur arrosé (1895), a staged joke about a gardener soaked by his own hose, was also a planned little story, so the fairer claim is that Guy was among the very first to make fiction films and the first woman to direct. Dating her La Fée aux Choux is hard because the 1896 original is lost and later remakes were long confused with it. D. W. Griffith was once praised as the man who 'invented' film grammar; scholars now point out that cross-cutting, close-ups and location shooting appeared earlier, in films by Porter, by British filmmakers such as G. A. Smith and James Williamson, and by others, and that Griffith's real achievement was combining and refining them. The Birth of a Nation raises a different kind of question: how to study a film that was technically important and enormously popular while also spreading racist propaganda that helped bring back the Ku Klux Klan. Most historians today discuss both facts together, and the NAACP's 1915 campaign against it is now seen as an early landmark in protests about media representation. Statistics about lost films are also debated. The Library of Congress's 2013 report by David Pierce was the first systematic count for American silent features: of 10,919 titles, 14 percent survive complete in original 35mm, 11 percent complete in other versions, 5 percent incomplete, and 70 percent completely lost. The often-repeated older claim that half of all American films made before 1950 are lost had, as the report itself notes, gained its authority mainly through repetition; sound films of the 1930s and 1940s survived much better because studios had a reason to copy them for television. Finally, Méliès's 'jammed camera' story is best treated as his own colourful origin myth: substitution tricks were also being explored by others, including in the Edison film The Execution of Mary Stuart (1895), which used a stop to swap an actor for a dummy before a beheading.
funFact: When the hand-coloured print of A Trip to the Moon was found in 1993, its nitrate film had decayed so badly that restorers needed many years, and about a million dollars, to rescue it, and it was finally shown at Cannes in 2011.
